lead: Programs that only run top-to-bottom are the exception, not the rule. Control flow — `if`, `switch`, loops, `break`, and the rest — is how you make a program that branches on conditions, repeats work until a goal is met, and stops cleanly when something goes wrong. After this chapter you will be able to write every major control-flow construct in C++, understand the pitfalls that trip up even experienced programmers, and use `<random>` to introduce controlled randomness into your programs.

aids.title: Dangling else: grammar overrides indentation
aids.md: In `if (a) if (b) doThing(); else doOther();` the `else` binds to the *nearest* unmatched `if` — that is `if (b)`, not `if (a)` — even though the indentation suggests otherwise. The compiler reads grammar, not whitespace. Use braces around every `if` body to make the attachment explicit and match what you actually intend.

aids.title: case labels do not create a new scope
aids.md: The entire body of a `switch` is one scope — `case` labels are just signposts inside it, not block boundaries. If you declare `int value` in one `case`, it is technically in scope for every `case` below, which can cause initialization and redeclaration surprises. The fix is a pair of braces around each `case` body that needs its own local variable.

aids.title: Half-open ranges and off-by-one errors
aids.md: C++ loops almost universally use a *half-open* range: start at `0`, stop when `i < count` (not `i <= count - 1`). The loop `for (int i { 0 }; i <= 10; ++i)` runs **eleven** times (0 through 10), not ten. Picture `[0, 10)` — the left bracket is closed (0 is included) and the right parenthesis is open (10 is excluded) — and you will almost never miscalculate an iteration count again.

aids.title: Seed once, reuse the engine
aids.md: Creating a new `std::mt19937` inside a loop resets the generator's state on every iteration, so you get the *same* first value every time the loop runs. Create and seed the engine exactly once, outside the loop, and the state advances naturally across calls — giving you a genuinely varied sequence.
